original_question: For nonlinear Schrodinger equations on graphs whose nonlinearity is close to the integrable cubic case but not exactly cubic, are the outgoing waves produced by vertex scattering still close to solitons over timescales comparable to those proved in the integrable cubic setting?
target_in_paper: The unlabeled conjectural remark at the end of Section 2.4, immediately after Lemma 2.4, about extending the cubic fast-soliton scattering picture to nonlinearities close to the integrable cubic NLS.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the right open direction: the paper asks whether the post-collision outgoing waves in the fast-soliton scattering problem on a graph should remain close to solitons when one perturbs away from the exactly integrable cubic case. It also correctly emphasizes the two key features of the cubic theory that matter here: soliton-like outgoing waves and a comparable validity timescale.
missing_details: The paper is not speaking about arbitrary graphs, but about the fast-soliton scattering problem on a three-edge star graph, i.e. a Y-junction, in Section 2.4.
The relevant regime is a single fast incoming soliton initially placed far from the vertex on one edge; the large-velocity hypothesis is essential.
In the exposition of Section 2.4 the vertex condition is Kirchhoff, even though nearby remarks note that some extensions to other selfadjoint boundary conditions may be possible.
The equation under discussion is the focusing NLS, and the cubic nonlinearity is singled out because integrability is used essentially in the proof of the cubic outgoing-wave approximation.
The post-interaction picture is more specific than generic 'outgoing waves': on a Y-junction it is one reflected pulse on the incoming edge and two transmitted pulses on the other edges.

The paper's rigorous graph-level control in this part is in L^2 (mass norm), not an unspecified notion of closeness; the paper explicitly contrasts this with stronger H^1-profile control in the line model it cites.
The timescale should be tied to the same post-interaction fast-soliton timescale proved in the cubic setting, not just any long timescale.
The phrase 'nonlinearities close to integrable' is informal in the paper; it does not specify a precise perturbative class such as nearby power nonlinearities or cubic-quintic perturbations.
The paper presents this as a conjectural/open extension, not as a theorem already established in arXiv:1304.1182.
refined_question: In the fast-soliton scattering setting of Section 2.4 for the focusing NLS on a three-edge star graph (Y-junction) with Kirchhoff coupling—starting from a single large-velocity soliton initially localized on one edge and impinging on the vertex—does an analogous post-collision description remain valid for nonlinearities that are sufficiently close to, but not exactly, the integrable cubic nonlinearity? More precisely, can one prove that, for all sufficiently large incoming velocities, the exact solution after the interaction is approximated in the same L^2 sense as in the cubic result by one reflected and two transmitted outgoing solitary waves, throughout a post-interaction timescale comparable to that proved in the cubic integrable case?
justification: The draft is clearly targeting the final open-direction remark in Section 2.4 rather than the standing-wave material earlier in the paper. The surrounding context of Section 2.4 fixes the model to fast-soliton scattering for cubic focusing NLS on a Y-junction, with Kirchhoff coupling and a single incoming fast soliton on one edge. Lemma 2.4 is the cubic benchmark: it gives the post-interaction approximation by outgoing soliton-like pieces, while the following remarks state that the proof uses the integrability of cubic NLS in an essential way, that the graph estimate is in L^2, and then explicitly raise the conjectural extension to nonlinearities close to integrable. The refined question therefore keeps exactly that benchmark and asks only whether it persists under a small non-integrable perturbation of the cubic nonlinearity, without broadening to other graphs, to arbitrary initial data, or to unrelated asymptotic problems.
